video_title: What Bessent Is Really Doing in the Bond Market | Mike Green
gist: Mike Green (CEO/CIO of the newly launched Tier 1 Alpha Asset Management) argues the global long-end bond selloff is a market-structure artifact, not a credit or inflation verdict: passive bond index funds weight by market capitalization, so they systematically under-buy deeply discounted low-coupon long bonds that are mathematically guaranteed to pull to par. In that frame, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's buyback program is simple, rational debt management — retiring roughly $2 of low-coupon paper for every $1 of current-coupon issuance — and the real policy error is a Fed keeping rates high, which Green says is itself inflationary via suppressed housing and auto supply. He also lays out his 'passive-aware investing' framework, the K-shaped/generational split between macro resilience and household depletion, and why gold is richly priced but likely still rising.

themes.theme: Passive bond indexing and the vanished duration buyer

insights.claim: The global long-end bond selloff reflects the absence of a price-sensitive marginal buyer rather than deteriorating credit: the marginal buyer is now a passive bond index fund that matches notional index exposure and ignores value entirely.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: If duration weakness is a flow/structure artifact rather than a credit event, long-end selloffs are a mean-reversion opportunity rather than a solvency warning.
insights.quote: what I think we're largely seeing right now is a global phenomenon in which duration is selling off because there is an absence of the marginal buyer of the longerdated bond

insights.claim: Because market-cap weighting is price times notional, a bond whose price has fallen gets a smaller index weight, so passive funds mechanically reduce demand for exactly the deeply discounted low-coupon bonds that offer the best expected return.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: The mechanism creates a persistent, exploitable bid/offer asymmetry: discounted long bonds stay orphaned until a non-index buyer (Treasury, levered accounts, or active managers) shows up.
insights.quote: as that price has fallen, their demand for those bonds has decreased on a relative basis. This creates the perception that nobody wants the bond, but the players at the game are behaving somewhat irrationally.

insights.claim: For high-quality bonds the price comparison passive funds make is nonsensical, because a bond at 50 and a bond at 150 both redeem at par — favoring the 150 bond means choosing to lose roughly a third of capital instead of doubling it.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Quantifies the structural edge available to anyone willing to own deep-discount long paper against the index-driven flow.
insights.quote: what we know about the bond trading at 50 and the bond trading at 150 is they're both going to end up at par

insights.claim: Bond markets are only about 15% passive by assets, but passive vehicles account for roughly 50% of marginal buying activity — the share that actually sets prices at the margin — versus roughly 55% passive in equities.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: The commonly cited 15% passive share understates fixed-income distortion by more than 3x; price formation in bonds is already as passive-dominated as equities.
insights.quote: equities are around 55% passive bond markets are only about 15% passive but that understates the influence that they have on the marginal activity where they're something closer to 50% of the marginal buying activity

insights.claim: Deeply discounted long-dated low-coupon bonds carry strong positive convexity that passive buyers ignore, offering the potential for capital to roughly double.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Frames deep-discount long bonds as an asymmetric long-convexity trade, not just a yield play.
insights.quote: They have positive convexity to the top side. Your money can literally double in many of these longdated bonds.

insights.claim: The 'Costanza market' pathology Green identified in equities around 2016 — where prices do the opposite of what fundamentals imply — has now migrated to the bond market.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Signals that fundamental bond analysis will keep producing wrong-way signals until flow analysis is layered on top.
insights.quote: Equity investors will remember this time as roughly around 2016 where we began to refer to the Castanza market, the market that did the opposite of what you thought it should

insights.claim: Japanese life insurers withdrew from global long-end buying not because foreign yields fell but because they hit their own actuarial threshold — roughly 2% — once domestic Japanese rates reached that level, removing a major structural bid from Western duration.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Watch JGB yields as the trigger variable: a fall back below ~2% in Japan would restore an offshore bid for US and European duration.
insights.quote: for Japanese life insurers, they don't care that bond yields are 5%. What they actually care is is that they have an actuarial requirement to meet their obligations. And the threshold for that was somewhere around 2%.

insights.claim: Green treats bond index investors as adversaries rather than peers, arguing both traders and the debt issuer should deliberately exploit their mandated indifference to price.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: An explicit statement that the largest fixed-income buyer is structurally exploitable — the core premise behind both the Treasury's buybacks and Green's own fund.
insights.quote: They are my opponent in this game.

insights.claim: The Treasury can issue $1 of current-coupon paper to retire roughly $2 of low-coupon discount paper, modestly raising cash interest expense while materially shrinking total outstanding debt.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: The buyback program is a debt-reduction arbitrage, not a rescue operation; expect it to be scaled up while long bonds trade at deep discounts.
insights.quote: we can issue $1 of current coupon paper and retire $2 of low coupon paper that has a modest increase in our cash interest expense but in aggregate we are significantly shrinking the debt

insights.claim: Green expects Bessent to keep shrinking the national debt while simultaneously pushing low-coupon bond prices higher, which itself attracts the market-cap-weighted passive buyer back into those bonds — a self-reinforcing loop.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: A second-order tailwind: Treasury buying raises prices, which raises index weights, which pulls in passive demand — a reason to front-run buyback-eligible discount CUSIPs.
insights.quote: he begins driving the prices of that national debt higher and attracting that marginal buyer with greater intensity

insights.claim: Criticism of Bessent is misdirected because the Treasury Secretary controls neither tax policy nor spending policy — his only lever over outlays is the interest cost of debt, given rates set by markets and the Fed.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Reframes 'Treasury intervention' headlines as noise; the fiscal risk premium, if any, should be priced off Congress, not Treasury operations.
insights.quote: He doesn't control tax policy. He doesn't control spending policy. In fact, the only spending policy he controls is how much the US government pays on its interest

insights.claim: Treating the August buyback expansion as a financial scandal is absurd; it is a voluntary exchange under an existing program and amounts to ordinary liability management, analogous to a household consolidating credit card debt at the lowest available rate.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Fading the 'debt-monetization scandal' narrative was the correct trade around the August announcement.
insights.quote: Scott is sitting there with a tourniquet saying, "Do you want me to put it on or not?"

insights.claim: The buyback program does not constitute classic yield curve control, which would require the Fed and Treasury to conspire to pin rates at a set level — Green sees no evidence of that yet, though the label would apply if the Fed steps in to assist.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete tripwire for when the YCC label becomes real: explicit Fed participation alongside Treasury buybacks.
insights.quote: yield curve control in the classic sense of the Federal Reserve and the Treasury conspire in order to keep rates artificially at a certain level. There's no sign that that's what we're engaged in at this point.

themes.theme: High rates as an inflation source

insights.claim: Keeping policy rates high to fight inflation is itself inflationary because it suppresses homebuilding and auto production, tightening the supply of shelter and used vehicles and holding rents and prices above where they would otherwise be.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: If correct, rate cuts would be disinflationary via supply response — inverting the standard playbook for positioning in homebuilders, rate-sensitive credit, and breakevens.
insights.quote: By keeping interest rates high in an attempt to forestall inflation, you are preventing new homes from being built.

insights.claim: The Fed's implied strategy — hold rates high until something breaks, then cut rapidly into the wreckage — is described by Green as actively bad policy rather than a considered plan.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Implies fat-tailed rate volatility: a long period of stubbornly high rates followed by a violent easing cycle, favoring convexity over carry.
insights.quote: That's the equivalent of saying, you know, well, I'm going to keep feeding my teenager drinks until they feel responsible enough to hand me the keys to the car.

insights.claim: High policy rates function as net stimulus to high-net-worth households through interest income, which is why dollar-weighted economic data looks resilient even as median households deteriorate.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Explains why aggregate spending data keeps surprising to the upside; cuts would remove that stimulus to the top cohort and could hit luxury/high-end consumption.

insights.claim: Green expects the Fed eventually to recognize it needs to cut rates, and cites that anticipated shift as a reason gold ultimately breaks higher.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Links the gold call directly to a Fed pivot: real-rate compression is the catalyst to watch for a gold breakout.
insights.quote: I do think that the Federal Reserve will get its act together and recognize that they need to cut interest rates

insights.claim: CPI's owners' equivalent rent methodology was created specifically to stop the Fed from repeating the early-1980s Volcker-era error of generating its own inflation through mortgage-rate passthrough, yet today the resulting three-to-five-year lagged average is again driving the same mistaken policy.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Argues headline CPI is a badly lagged signal, so trading the print as a real-time inflation read is a structural error.
insights.quote: That is where the owner's equivalent rent came in. It basically was created to prevent the Federal Reserve from doing something as stupid as it did.

insights.claim: The pandemic-era policy mix — shutting the economy, then papering it over with fiscal transfers and easy mortgage financing in 2020-2021 — predictably financed a demand surge for living space and should not have been accommodated for as long as it was.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Roots current housing unaffordability in a policy choice rather than a supply shock, supporting the view that shelter inflation is policy-reversible.

themes.theme: Market prices refute the fiscal-doom narrative

insights.claim: US sovereign CDS has contracted over recent months, contradicting claims that the long-end selloff reflects deteriorating US credit quality or expected dollar debasement.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable falsification test: if a debt crisis were being priced, US CDS would widen — it hasn't.
insights.quote: So, a massive depreciation of the dollar would show up as an increase in US CDS that has failed to materialize. In fact, US CDS has contracted over the past several months.

insights.claim: Inflation swaps and breakevens — the instruments that would register inflation fear — are not showing it, undercutting the inflation explanation for the long-end selloff.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Second falsification test; the absence of a breakeven move argues term-premium/flow, not inflation, is driving long yields.

insights.claim: Australia, with debt-to-GDP around 25%, is experiencing the same long-end bond selloff as the US at over 100%, proving the phenomenon is a global market-structure event rather than a US fiscal verdict.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: The single cleanest cross-sectional test against the fiscal-sustainability story — and a reason to expect the same distortion in every developed long-end market.
insights.quote: Well, then we'd have to look over to Australia, which has debt to GDP of 25% and is experiencing the exact same bond market sell-off.

insights.claim: The arithmetic of fixing the US deficit is trivial — marginally raise revenue and marginally cut spending until the deficit falls below nominal GDP growth so debt/GDP shrinks — and the binding constraint is political will, specifically unwillingness to ask system beneficiaries to give up a little.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Positions the fiscal question as a political-risk trade rather than a solvency trade; watch tax policy, not Treasury auctions.
insights.quote: You marginally increase your revenue and you marginally decrease your spending. And guess what? that unsustainable deficit will disappear or at least fall below the nominal growth rate of the US economy

insights.claim: The apocalyptic Treasury-market narrative originates in a broad loss of faith in US institutions and a search for someone to blame, not in observable market pricing.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Sentiment-driven narratives that markets do not confirm tend to create mispricing — a reason to lean against consensus doom positioning.
insights.quote: They are rats trapped in a cage being randomly subjected to shocks from their perspective and they're looking for somebody to blame.

insights.claim: Green expects society to demand a scapegoat and suspects a market event will ultimately be the mechanism that forces the hard fiscal and social choices being avoided today.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: A crisis is his base case as the forcing function for reform, without a named catalyst or date — argues for holding tail hedges rather than timing.
insights.quote: my strong hunch is that market events will actually force us at some point to make the harder choices that we have been avoiding up to this point

themes.theme: Household depletion and the shifting center

insights.claim: Hard economic data votes with dollars while soft data votes one household per vote, so as wealth concentrates the hard data increasingly reflects only the top cohort while soft data captures the median household's actual experience.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Argues the profession's dismissal of soft data is a systematic blind spot — sentiment surveys may lead consumption breaks even when spending looks fine.
insights.quote: In the soft data, we're getting the picture of what the median person gets. Like a democracy, it is one person or one household and one vote.

insights.claim: Rising prices for necessities force stressed households to deplete savings and take on debt, which registers as increased spending and economic activity even as those households are financially sinking.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Consumption strength driven by necessity-financed borrowing is a fragility indicator, not a resilience indicator — watch subprime credit and savings rates.

insights.claim: The endgame of household depletion is 'household consolidation' — moving in with parents — which produces a sudden, catastrophic step-down in aggregate spending rather than a gradual slowdown, and survey respondents report they are getting closer to that breaking point.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Flags a discontinuous, non-linear consumption risk that trend-following macro models will miss; negative for rental housing, utilities volumes, and low-end retail.
insights.quote: That is a catastrophic reduction of spending that is created once people hit a breaking point.

insights.claim: Institutional investors have openly adopted 'we only invest in what is sold to the top of the K' as a stated strategy, which Green says is understandable but is itself accelerating the decay of public trust.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Confirms the top-of-K trade is now crowded consensus among multi-managers — a caution flag for luxury and premium-consumer positioning.
insights.quote: many pod shops and investors now say we only invest in stuff that is sold to the top of the K

insights.claim: The divide is generational as much as income-based: high asset prices preserve older cohorts' purchasing power while making housing and family formation unaffordable for younger ones, and government ROI analysis on its own social programs shows far higher returns from programs like Head Start than from end-of-life medical spending.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: A political-economy case that asset-price support is a policy choice with a constituency — and one that unusual election outcomes suggest is starting to erode.
insights.quote: you consistently have made the choice at every step in the process to protect your circumstances without considering how that's affecting other people's circumstances through time

insights.claim: Green argues AI chatbots push users toward the center in a way search engines never did, because search monetizes by serving ads matched to the query while AI attempts a holistic answer.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: A non-obvious second-order implication: mass AI adoption could depolarize opinion formation and, by extension, dilute the influence of narrative-driven interests in markets.
insights.quote: it's going to try to give you a more holistic answer. That naturally forces people towards the center.

insights.claim: Surprising election outcomes in states assumed to be safely red or blue indicate the political tails are far weaker than believed and that a large homogeneous center can flip either direction with disturbing frequency.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Argues against pricing durable one-party policy regimes into long-horizon positions ahead of the midterms.
insights.quote: What there actually is is a relatively homogeneous center and that homogeneous center can flip 50/50 in either direction with disturbing frequency

insights.claim: Green describes himself as simultaneously insanely bearish and insanely optimistic: the outcomes he fears stem from society's own reversible choices rather than external forces, so diagnosis is the precondition for improvement.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Clarifies that his crash thesis is conditional on policy inertia, not a fatalistic call — the bearish positioning has an exit condition.
insights.quote: I come across depending on how you want to listen to me as insanely bearish or insanely optimistic. And the answer is both.

insights.claim: The 1978 shift from defined-benefit pensions to self-insured defined-contribution plans destroyed the statistical pooling of longevity risk, forcing every individual to hedge the right-tail risk of living a very long time.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Roots the entire passive-flow distortion in a single 1978 policy change that will not be reversed quickly — meaning the flow tailwind persists for years.
insights.quote: A pension that is spread across 100,000 participants has very different cash flow characteristics than those individual 100,000 people

insights.claim: Individually self-insured longevity risk structurally advantages equities over debt and raises the real cost of borrowing for debt issuers.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Provides a structural explanation for persistently rich equity valuations and cheap-looking long bonds that is independent of the business cycle.
insights.quote: you structurally advantage equities over debt and you raise the relative real cost of debt and debt and the cost for debt issuers

insights.claim: The market-cap-weighted bond index methodology was blessed by the Department of Labor, not the Treasury, so fixing it requires a separate cabinet-level regulatory process and likely an act of Congress against Wall Street's largest lobbyists — making reform unrealistic.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Confirms the distortion is durable: no near-term regulatory fix, so the trade based on it has a long runway.

insights.claim: There is no such thing as a free-market price — prices are always set inside a regulatory framework — so the passive bond distortion should be treated as a permanent feature of the rulebook rather than an anomaly awaiting correction.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: A mental model for sizing structural trades: understand the rules that produce the flow rather than waiting for prices to 'normalize'.
insights.quote: if you go to a Moroccan souk, I guarantee you that there are rules around how you get to set up a stall in that Moroccan souk

insights.claim: Green's intellectual breakthrough roughly a year ago was recognizing that the fund is a distinct entity from its underlying securities — a distinction he says is essentially absent from academic finance literature, which treats securities as the end recipients of capital.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Identifies a documented gap in mainstream models that Green claims is the source of his edge — the reason to take his flow-based forecasts seriously.
insights.quote: I had not understood that the fund was distinct from the underlying securities.

insights.claim: Tier 1 Alpha aggregates fund-level flow information down into each individual security; compute time per security went from about 45 minutes in September of last year to about 45 seconds in January and is now under one second, enabling full-index coverage and repeated flow-scenario modeling.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: A concrete capability timeline showing the strategy only became implementable in 2026 — an argument that this edge is not yet arbitraged away.
insights.quote: in January, we got it down to about 45 seconds. We're now sub one second on each security.

insights.claim: Green estimates the 'passive factor' explains roughly 50% of the price move of any individual security today, making it the single most important driver of price behavior.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: If half of single-stock return variance is flow-driven, traditional factor models are misspecified and flow data is the highest-value input available.
insights.quote: In general, we think it explains about 50% of the price move of any individual security at this point.

insights.claim: Traditional fundamental analysis works by predicting the behavior of similarly-trained investors, so as that active cohort shrinks and experiences outflows, classic fundamental signals acquire negative loading and predict net selling rather than buying.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Explains why good fundamental calls keep losing money and argues signals must be re-signed or combined with flow data to remain useful.
insights.quote: I'm increasingly watching a marginal pool of the population that actually in aggregate is experiencing outflows. And so all of those insights have actually negative loading factors.

insights.claim: Green's crowd-and-fire-hose analogy reframes the analytical question: traditional fundamentals are like knowing a crowd's FICO scores and marital status, when what predicts the reaction to a wall of liquidity is how much each member weighs and whether they are steady on their feet.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: A usable mental model: for flow-driven markets, measure a security's liquidity elasticity, not its business quality.
insights.quote: But they tell me absolutely nothing about how that crowd is going to react when hit with a wall of liquidity.

insights.claim: Shrinking active management acts like chaperones who now only appear at predictable intervals, producing an alternating rhythm of unusually calm markets and sudden blowups, with active managers eventually just shutting the doors rather than restoring order.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Predicts a persistent volatility regime of long suppression punctuated by violent gaps — favorable for owning convexity, punishing for short-vol carry.
insights.quote: that actually perversely creates conditions under which the party appears totally tame and then it goes totally crazy and totally tame and totally crazy

insights.claim: Green still expects the passive dynamic to end very badly for equities and has embedded that view in his products, but is deliberately launching with a small active bet against US large-cap indices rather than a levered maximum-expression version.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: His long-standing passive-unwind crash thesis is unchanged; the product design is a distribution choice, not a softening of the view.
insights.quote: No, I still think that ultimately this is going to end very badly.

insights.claim: Active management has abandoned the center of investor portfolios and crowded into roughly $1.5 trillion of 'hot sauce' niche products, as Eric Okun predicted about five years ago — leaving the core S&P 500 allocation, typically 35-40% of a portfolio, uncontested.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Identifies where competitive capital is not deployed — the core equity allocation — as the largest underexploited commercial and alpha opportunity in asset management.
insights.quote: the active management community has basically focused itself on a tiny sliver of about a trillion and a half dollars of possible assets

themes.theme: Gold, TIPS and the trust discount

insights.claim: A 30-year TIPS currently offers about a 3% real yield, which delivers nearly the entire 4% safe-withdrawal rule inflation-protected for 30 years with no principal risk — and almost nobody wants it.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: The most concrete actionable idea in the episode: a near-riskless solution to the retirement-income problem that investor psychology is currently rejecting.
insights.quote: things like a 30-year tip currently offering a 3% real yield which extraordinary to stop and think about a 4% withdrawal yield, 4% withdrawal rule

insights.claim: Rejecting TIPS in favor of gold requires believing not only that the dollar will be debased but that the US government will systematically falsify inflation statistics — a two-step assumption most gold advocates do not state explicitly.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Isolates the actual load-bearing assumption in the debasement trade, letting investors test whether they truly hold it.
insights.quote: you're saying not only do I think the dollar will be worthless I think the US government is going to lie to me every step of the way

insights.claim: Gold is the ultimate negative-trust asset because it carries no counterparty obligation and requires nothing from anyone else to retain its value — unlike wheat, which needs storage, guarding and processing before it has use value.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Explains why gold, not broad commodities, is the correct instrument for expressing a loss-of-institutional-trust view.
insights.quote: There's nothing that anyone else has to do for it to remain gold.

insights.claim: Green endorses Jim Grant's definition of gold as 1/n where n is faith in central bankers, and says gold's multiple rises as that faith falls.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Gives a single tradeable variable for the gold thesis: track credibility of central banks, not inflation prints.
insights.quote: Jim Grant I think still has the best definition of gold as one over n where n is faith in central bankers

insights.claim: On the classic gold-buys-a-fine-suit metric gold is roughly 400% overvalued, since Green's custom suits cost around $1,200 — yet he still expects gold to keep responding higher because policymakers are not yet making good policy.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: A rare 'expensive but going higher' formulation: own gold for the policy-failure catalyst, not for valuation support.
insights.quote: So, gold is somewhere around 400% overvalued on that metric.

insights.claim: The 2022 US decision to seize Russian assets drove reserve managers out of Treasuries and into gold, temporarily breaking gold's historical link to real interest rates — a marginal-buyer effect analogous to passive flows, not a permanent regime change.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Warns against extrapolating gold's decoupling from real rates; the relationship reasserts when that marginal buyer stops buying.
insights.quote: We can no longer hold treasuries because they are no longer a safe asset. The US government has indicated they will seize them

insights.claim: Middle Eastern buyers, squeezed by war-driven defense and social spending while restrained oil production limits their benefit from high oil prices, have been forced into selling gold — suppressing the price relative to what real rates alone would imply.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific seller currently capping gold; a Middle East de-escalation or oil-price surge would remove that overhang.

insights.claim: Retail rotation into commodities is an outward shift in aggregate demand borrowed from the future that raises near-term prices, and high central bank rates then retard the production response that would normally resolve the shortage — requiring even higher prices to clear.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Explains a self-reinforcing commodity price spiral under tight policy, and why the commodity trade can work for the 'wrong' reasons before violently reversing.

insights.claim: Commodities are a poor inflation hedge for most households because they represent a tiny share of actual consumption expenditure — auto depreciation dwarfs gasoline spending, and child care dwarfs corn, grain and oil combined.
insights.speaker: Mike Green
insights.so_what: Undercuts the standard case for a large retail commodity allocation as a cost-of-living hedge.
insights.quote: even at today's elevated gasoline expenditures, you are spending far more on the depreciation of the vehicle than you are on the actual gas that you're consuming
